references.text: Jesus was called a 'Nazarene' – [ref:Matt 2:23|Matthew 2:23] tells us that Joseph settled in Nazareth so that what was spoken through the prophets might be fulfilled, namely that he would be called a Nazarene. The term 'Ναζωραῖος' in Luke 18:37 links Jesus to his hometown of Nazareth.
In [ref:Matt 21:11|Matthew 21:11], the crowd identifies Jesus as 'the prophet from Nazareth in Galilee.' Similarly, in Luke 18:37, the crowd identifies Jesus as 'the Nazarene' as he passes by.
In [ref:Luk 4:16|Luke 4:16], it is told that Jesus came to Nazareth, where he had grown up. This is the background for why people called him 'Jesus of Nazareth' (Ναζωραῖος), as they do in Luke 18:37.

In [ref:Joh 1:45-46|John 1:45–46], Philip refers to Jesus as 'him from Nazareth,' and Nathanael asks whether anything good can come from Nazareth. The term 'Nazarene' was thus a well-known identifier for Jesus.
In [ref:Joh 18:5-7|John 18:5–7], the soldiers identify the one they are seeking as 'Jesus of Nazareth' (Ἰησοῦν τὸν Ναζωραῖον) – exactly the same designation used in Luke 18:37.
In [ref:Apg 2:22|Acts 2:22], Peter refers to Jesus as 'Jesus of Nazareth' (Ἰησοῦν τὸν Ναζωραῖον) in his Pentecost sermon. The term was used as a fixed identifier for Jesus in early preaching.

In [ref:Luk 18:36|Luke 18:36], the blind man heard that a crowd was passing by and asked what it was. Verse 37 is the answer he received – that it was Jesus of Nazareth who was passing by. The verse provides the immediate context.

In [ref:Luk 18:38-39|Luke 18:38–39], the blind man cries out, 'Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!' in response to the information in verse 37. He recognizes Jesus as the Messiah and uses the messianic title 'Son of David' instead of simply 'Nazarene.'
The parallel passage in [ref:Mark 10:47|Mark 10:47] tells us that the blind man Bartimaeus heard that it was 'Jesus of Nazareth' and began to shout. Mark gives the same scene with a few more details.
